1289.title: the three doshas as a way of noticing, not a diagnosis
1289.word: the three doshas as a way of noticing
1289.hook: a day has moods that arrive roughly on schedule. one classical text gives each stretch of time a dosha
1289.carry: the three doshas as a way of noticing, not a diagnosis
1289.tomorrow: the three doshas as a way of noticing, not a diagnosis
1289.howItsDone: Ayurvedic teaching links kapha, pitta and vata to the beginning, middle and end of a day, a night, a meal and a life; on this path that pattern is used only for noticing, never to diagnose.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the three doshas as a way of noticing, and Sushruta's word for well: svastha, a definition that ends in a clear, content mind.

Early morning, the body is slow to get going, and the snooze button looks very reasonable. Around noon, hunger gets sharp, and so does the temper. Late afternoon, attention starts to scatter like leaves in a parking lot. A day has moods, and they tend to arrive roughly on schedule. The Ashtanga Hridaya noticed a pattern like that too. It doesn't hand out a timetable to the minute. It gives each part of the day a dosha.

In paraphrase, the verse says this. The doshas run through the whole body, and they rise in turn: kapha at the beginning, pitta in the middle, vata at the end. The beginning, middle and end of what? Of a life, of a day, of a night, and of a meal. One three-part pattern, laid over four clocks. Take the day: at its beginning kapha, the heavy, slow, steady one; in the middle pitta, the hot and sharp; toward the end vata, the light and moving. Over a life it reads the same way: kapha in childhood, pitta in the middle years, vata in old age. Over a meal: heaviness right after eating, then the heat of digestion, then lightness. Notice what the verse doesn't say. It gives no exact hours; beginning, middle and end are all it offers, and how anyone divides those up is a later question. And notice the tone. The doshas are simply taking turns, the way the light changes across a day. That's the gift for noticing. A slow morning may not be a character flaw. A sharp noon may not be a personal failing. Some of it may be the hour. On this path, that's a way of looking, not a rule to live by, and never a diagnosis. Anything about sleep or energy that keeps on is a question for a doctor.
screen: `BEGINNING, MIDDLE, END.` · `A LIFE, A DAY, A NIGHT, A MEAL.` · `KAPHA, THEN PITTA, THEN VATA.` · `NO HOURS: JUST THE TURNS.`

segments.voice: Notice what part of the day it is right now: beginning, middle or end. Then look for that part's quality in your body: heaviness, heat, or lightness and a skittering mind. Don't judge what you find; just notice whether the hour and the body agree today, or rest in prayer if you pray.
The three doshas, as a way of noticing, not a diagnosis. Today, on the clock: kapha at the beginning, pitta in the middle, vata at the end.

1290.title: the three doshas as a way of noticing, not a diagnosis
1290.word: the three doshas as a way of noticing
1290.hook: warm water into a warm bath makes it warmer. the Charaka Samhita builds a way of seeing on that plain rule
1290.carry: the three doshas as a way of noticing, not a diagnosis
1290.tomorrow: the three doshas as a way of noticing, not a diagnosis
1290.howItsDone: Ayurvedic physicians draw on the principle that like increases like and opposites decrease when they work with a patient; on this path the principle is used only to notice what is stacking up, never to treat anything.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the three doshas as a way of noticing, on the clock: kapha at the beginning, pitta in the middle, vata at the end.

Run warm water into a warm bath and it gets warmer. Add cold, and it cools down. Pile a second blanket on the first and the bed gets heavier. Nobody needs a textbook for any of that. The Charaka Samhita, one of Ayurveda's classical texts, sets down that same plain logic near its very beginning, and then builds a whole way of seeing on top of it. Today: like adds to like.
screen: `WARM INTO WARM.` → `COLD INTO WARM.` → `A SECOND BLANKET.`

segments.voice: In paraphrase, the rule is this: for all things, at all times, the similar is the cause of increase, and the dissimilar is the cause of decrease. Like adds to like. Unlike takes away. Put that next to the qualities from a few days ago and it becomes a noticing tool. A cold, windy day, a skipped lunch, a rush between three errands: cold on cold, light on light, moving on moving. Vata's qualities stack up, and by evening the stack can be felt. Or a hot bus ride, a kitchen with every burner going, a tense meeting: heat on heat on heat. Or a long, cloudy Sunday, a second helping, an extra hour on the couch: heavy on heavy. The other half of the rule is just as plain. Something warm meets something cold, and the cold eases. Steadiness meets scatter, and the scatter settles. Here is where care matters. In the classical tradition, this rule guides trained physicians, who work case by case. On this path it does something smaller. It doesn't tell anyone what to eat, what to take, or how to treat anything. It's a question to ask: what's stacking up today? Just seeing the stack can be enough for one day. And if something is actually wrong, that's for a doctor.
screen: `SIMILAR INCREASES, UNLIKE DECREASES.` · `DRY ON DRY, HEAT ON HEAT.` · `HEAVY ON HEAVY.` · `SEE THE STACK. DON'T PRESCRIBE.`

segments.voice: Notice one quality that feels strong right now, heat, heaviness, dryness or rush, and see what else today shares it: the weather, a meal, a conversation. Then look for one opposite quality that's already here, a cool breath, a still hand, a lighter thought, and rest there without fixing anything. If you pray, you can rest in prayer here.
The three doshas, as a way of noticing, not a diagnosis. Today, with Charaka's rule: like adds to like, unlike takes away.

1291.title: the three doshas as a way of noticing, not a diagnosis
1291.word: the three doshas as a way of noticing
1291.hook: a river has banks that hold for years and a level that changes with every storm. the classical texts ask about both
1291.carry: the three doshas as a way of noticing, not a diagnosis
1291.tomorrow: the three doshas as a way of noticing, not a diagnosis
1291.howItsDone: Ayurvedic practitioners consider both a person's nature (prakriti) and their present state (vikriti); on this path there is no type quiz, and the doshas are used only to notice how today is.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the three doshas as a way of noticing, with Charaka's rule: like adds to like, unlike takes away, and a stack you can learn to see.

A river has a shape: its banks, its bends, the wide slow stretch below the bridge. That shape holds for years. A river also has a level, and the level changes with every storm and every dry spell. Ask someone what the river is like and they could describe either one, and both answers would be true. The classical Ayurveda texts keep those two questions apart when they look at a person. Today: nature, and today.
screen: `THE BANKS HOLD FOR YEARS.` → `THE LEVEL CHANGES WITH THE STORM.` → `TWO TRUE ANSWERS.`

segments.voice: The first question is prakriti: a person's nature, their constitution. The classical texts describe it as given from the start, the banks of the river. The Charaka Samhita describes people whose nature leans toward one dosha or another, with the qualities that go with it. The second question is vikriti: how things stand now, the departure from that nature, the water level after the storm. Prakriti is the banks. Vikriti can change by the afternoon. In the Charaka Samhita both appear among the things a physician examines in a patient: two questions kept side by side, not merged into one. Here's why that matters for noticing. It's easy to stop at the first question, take the answer, and wear it like a jersey. I'm pitta, so I'm intense. I'm kapha, so I'm slow. A label like that can explain everything and notice nothing. The second question keeps things moving: not who am I, forever, but how am I, today? Hot, after a rough morning? Scattered, after too little sleep? On this path there's no quiz to find anyone's type, and no diagnosis. The texts' own answer to the first question belongs to trained practitioners. The second, how is today, is one anyone can ask, any time, with nothing to prove.
screen: `PRAKRITI: A PERSON'S NATURE.` · `VIKRITI: HOW THINGS STAND NOW.` · `A LABEL CAN EXPLAIN AND NOT NOTICE.` · `NOT WHO AM I, BUT HOW AM I TODAY?`

segments.voice: Ask one plain question, how am I today, and let the answer come as qualities: moving or still, hot or cool, heavy or light. If a label shows up, I'm always like this, set it gently on the bank and come back to the water. If you pray, you can rest in prayer here.
The three doshas, as a way of noticing, not a diagnosis. Today, two questions kept apart: prakriti, a person's nature, and vikriti, how things stand now.
Your line: the three doshas as a way of noticing, not a diagnosis. The banks hold; the water moves. Same time tomorrow.

1292.title: the three doshas as a way of noticing, not a diagnosis
1292.word: the three doshas as a way of noticing
1292.hook: a tightrope walker's pole never stops moving; one line in the Ashtanga Hridaya puts health on the same wire
1292.carry: the three doshas as a way of noticing, not a diagnosis
1292.howItsDone: Ayurvedic practitioners describe health as the three doshas in balance and illness as their imbalance, and some people who follow Ayurveda use the idea to notice daily patterns alongside medical care, not in place of it.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the three doshas as a way of noticing took two questions: prakriti, the banks of the river, and vikriti, the water level after the storm.

A tightrope walker is never quite still. Watch the long pole in their hands: it dips a little left, a little right, catching each tilt before it turns into a fall. From the ground it looks like calm. Up on the wire it's a steady run of small corrections. Balance, up there, isn't a pose struck once and kept. It's done again and again. The Ashtanga Hridaya puts health on that same wire, in one short line. On the last of the dosha days: balance, not a type.
screen: `A POLE THAT NEVER STOPS MOVING.` → `SMALL CORRECTIONS.` → `ONE LINE ON BALANCE.`

segments.voice: Here is the line, in paraphrase: illness is the doshas out of balance; health is the doshas in balance. Two halves, each the mirror of the other. In Sanskrit the key words are vaishamya, unevenness, and samya, evenness. Look at what the line leaves out. It doesn't ask for less of any dosha. Vata, the moving one, still moves the breath. Pitta, the hot one, still digests the meal. Kapha, the steady one, still holds the body together. Health isn't one of them winning, or one being driven out. It's the three even with each other. And the line doesn't sort anyone into a vata person or a kapha person. It describes the three together, in balance or out of it, in any body. That gathers up the dosha days: the three as forces, their qualities, their turns on the clock, like adding to like, a nature that holds and a today that changes. Each was a way of seeing which way things are tipping. Here the title earns its second half. In the classical texts, judging an imbalance is a physician's work, done by examining a person closely. A lesson can't do that, and neither can a quiz. Pain, fever, a change that worries you: that goes to a doctor. What the line offers an ordinary day is smaller: not what's wrong with me, but what's tipping right now, and what small correction would bring it a little nearer the middle?
screen: `ILLNESS: THE DOSHAS UNEVEN` · `HEALTH: THE DOSHAS EVEN` · `ALL THREE STAY` · `NOTICING, NOT DIAGNOSING`

segments.voice: Sit upright, feet on the floor, and lean a little left, then a little right, like the walker's pole, each sway smaller than the last until you settle near the center. Feel the tiny adjustments that keep you upright, the ones you usually never notice. Then let the in-breath and the out-breath find about the same length, without forcing, or rest in prayer if you pray.
The three doshas, as a way of noticing, not a diagnosis. Illness is the three out of balance, health the three in balance: an evenness kept by small corrections.
Your line: the three doshas as a way of noticing, not a diagnosis. Balance is done again and again. See you tomorrow.

1293.title: the daily routine (dinacharya)
1293.hook: a toothbrush, a tongue, a clean shirt: a classical Ayurvedic text treats them as the ground of health
1293.howItsDone: People who follow Ayurveda keep a morning round described in the classical texts, such as cleaning the teeth, scraping the tongue, rinsing the mouth, oiling the body and bathing, often alongside a family's own morning worship.

segments.voice: Yesterday closed the three doshas as a way of noticing, not a diagnosis, with one line from the Ashtanga Hridaya: health is the three in balance.

A toothbrush sits in a cup by the sink. It's one of the least dramatic objects in a home. Nobody photographs it. And yet one of Ayurveda's classical texts, the Charaka Samhita, gives real space to exactly this kind of thing: cleaning the teeth, rinsing the mouth, washing, putting on clean clothes. Next to its teaching on the doshas and the body sits a careful description of an ordinary morning. Why would a text about health spend its words there?
screen: `A TOOTHBRUSH IN A CUP.` → `A CLASSICAL TEXT, AN ORDINARY MORNING.` → `WHY SPEND WORDS THERE?`

segments.voice: The Sanskrit name is dinacharya. Dina is day. Charya is a way of going about, a conduct. The day's conduct: the daily round. In the Charaka Samhita, the chapter on daily regimen begins with eating in the right measure, then walks through things anyone would recognize. Caring for the eyes. Cleaning the teeth with a twig. Scraping the tongue. Rinsing the mouth. Oil for the body. A bath. Clean clothes. Paraphrased, but the list really is that plain. The text doesn't ask for a heroic month. It asks for this morning, and then the next one. Health, in this picture, is less an event than a texture, woven out of small repeated acts. Repetition can be a gift: a routine you don't have to decide every time frees up attention. But the text lists these acts one by one, as if each is worth doing well, so there's an invitation inside the habit: now and then, do the ordinary thing on purpose. The routine has neighbors, too. In some Hindu homes the morning also has a bath before worship, a lamp lit, a prayer or a name said, and Ayurveda's daily round sits comfortably beside them. The next days show how far the texts let it reach, even into how a person speaks to others. None of this is a rule to pass or fail. It's a way of seeing a morning: not as the boring part before life starts, but as a place where life is already being looked after.

1294.title: the daily routine (dinacharya)
1294.hook: the first thing the hand reaches for in the morning; the classical daily round begins before dawn
1294.howItsDone: Some Hindus rise in brahma muhurta, the time before sunrise, for prayer, study or meditation, and Ayurvedic texts recommend waking then for a person in health.

segments.voice: Yesterday, the daily routine, dinacharya: the day's conduct, an ordinary morning walked step by step in the Charaka Samhita.

What does the hand reach for first in the morning? Often, the answer glows. Before the feet touch the floor, the day has already arrived from somewhere else: the news, the messages, somebody's argument from last night. The first minutes belong to everyone but the person waking up. The classical daily round starts somewhere very different. In the Ashtanga Hridaya, another of Ayurveda's classical texts, the chapter on the daily routine opens before the sun is up, with one small instruction about waking.
screen: `WHAT DOES THE HAND REACH FOR?` → `THE DAY ARRIVES FROM ELSEWHERE.` → `THE ROUND STARTS BEFORE THE SUN.`

segments.voice: Paraphrased, the verse says: a healthy person should rise in brahma muhurta, to protect their life. Brahma muhurta is the stretch of time before sunrise that Hindu tradition sets apart. Tradition reckons it from the sunrise, not from the clock, so it shifts with the seasons and the place. And the hour is prized beyond Ayurveda: tradition says it's a good time for prayer, for study, for meditation, while the house and the street are still quiet. Three things in the verse are worth slowing down for. Who it's for: the healthy person. It doesn't summon someone who is ill, or up all night with a baby, out of bed in the dark. The reason: not productivity, not getting ahead of everyone else, but to protect life. The early hour is framed as care, the way you'd guard something precious. And what comes next. The text doesn't send the waking person straight into tasks. Paraphrased again, it asks them first to consider the body, whether last night's food has been digested. The first act of the day is attention, turned inward. That's the part that travels, whatever time the alarm goes off. A night-shift worker, a new parent, a student who sleeps late can't all keep the dawn hour. But anyone can keep the first minute: arriving in the body before the day arrives from elsewhere.

1295.title: the daily routine (dinacharya)
1295.hook: eyes, nose, mouth, tongue, skin: the classical morning wakes the senses one by one
1295.howItsDone: People who follow Ayurveda's morning round tend the eyes, clean the teeth, scrape the tongue, rinse or gargle the mouth, and some use oil in the nose or on the body before bathing.

segments.voice: Yesterday the daily routine began before sunrise: rise in brahma muhurta to protect life, and ask the body first.

Lay the classical texts' morning care side by side and it covers a lot of ground in a small space: a tour of the face, eyes, nose, teeth, tongue and mouth, and then the skin, all of it. Read quickly, it's a hygiene checklist. Read slowly, it's a way of waking the senses up one at a time, so the person who walks out the door has actually arrived in their own body. It's also the end of the week, so a look back comes after.
screen: `EYES, NOSE, TEETH, TONGUE.` → `A TOUR OF THE FACE.` → `THE SENSES, ONE BY ONE.`

segments.voice: The Charaka Samhita and the Ashtanga Hridaya both walk through this morning care, each in its own order. Paraphrased: the eyes are tended. The teeth are cleaned with a twig, chewed into a soft brush. The tongue is scraped. The mouth is rinsed and gargled, sometimes with oil. Drops of oil may go in the nose. Then oil for the body, and a bath. Each of these is a door. The eyes see, the nose smells, the tongue tastes, the skin feels. And in Hindu thought the senses matter far beyond hygiene. The Gita, for one, pictures a steady person drawing the senses in, the way a tortoise draws in its limbs. The morning round doesn't preach about any of that. It just touches each door, gently, before the day starts knocking on all of them, from the head down, from small to whole: a twig for the teeth before oil for the whole body. Now the week. The doshas took their turns on the clock, stacked like on like, split into nature and today, and closed on health as the three in balance. Then the daily round opened: dina, day, charya, conduct. It rose before sunrise, in the verse at least, to protect life, and checked in with the body first. And today, the senses, woken one by one. The thread through all of it: Ayurveda keeps building health out of ordinary minutes.
screen: `EYES, TEETH, TONGUE, MOUTH, SKIN` · `EACH SENSE IS A DOOR` · `FROM THE HEAD DOWN, SMALL TO WHOLE` · `THE WEEK: ORDINARY MINUTES`

segments.voice: Without moving, soften the eyes and notice light and shape, then the nearest sound and the farthest. Then the air and any smell at all, the taste of your mouth right now, and the skin: clothes, air, the weight where you sit. Door by door, then let them rest together in the breath; if you pray, you can name each sense as a gift as you pass it.
